note: Lessons whose shared Learning Lab model teaches a neighbouring lesson's mathematics get their own Explore model here: either another lab model (kind lab-model + model) or a lesson explorer (assets/math-studio/<kind>.mjs). Read by scripts/lib/math-studio-registry.mjs. Defaults and contexts come from each lesson's own worked example (launch.conceptIntro.iDo). Audit 2026-11-16: 6-5, 2-1, 2-8, 2-11, 3-2, 3-9, 5-1, 5-4, 5-6, 5-10, 6-8, 6-13, 6-15.

6-5.title: Parts of an Expression
6-5.context: Tickets cost $12 each, plus a flat $50 venue fee. Let t be the number of tickets: total = 12t + 50.
6-5.contextEs: Los boletos cuestan $12 cada uno, más una tarifa fija de $50 por el lugar. Sea t el número de boletos: total = 12t + 50.
guide: Each colour is one part, and the brackets under the expression show its terms.
Change one box at a time and watch which part changes.
investigate: Before you change anything: in 12t + 50, which number grows the total each time t goes up by 1, and which number is added only once?
Set the coefficient to 1. Why does the expression show t and not 1t? What is the coefficient now?
Change the operation to −. Is 50 still the constant? Is it still a term?
Set the constant to 0. How many terms are left?
Evaluate for t = 0, 1 and 2. Which part tells you how much the total grows each time?

term.definition: A part of an expression joined to the other parts by + or −. A term can be a number (50), a variable (t), or a number times a variable (12t).
term.definitionEs: Una parte de una expresión que se une a las otras partes con + o −. Un término puede ser un número (50), una variable (t) o un número por una variable (12t).

6-5.lead: Meet the four parts of an expression one at a time, name them, then build and evaluate your own.

3-2.title: Unit Price
3-2.lead: Divide the price by the number of items to find the cost of one: the unit rate.
guide: Price divided by the number of items gives the unit price in dollars per item.
Change the price or the pack size and predict the unit price before reading it.
investigate: Booth A charges $3 for 5 games. Before you look: is one game more or less than $1?
Keep the price at $3 and double the games to 10. What happens to the cost of one game?
Find a pack size and price that cost exactly $0.50 per item.
A rate compares two different units. Name both units in “$3 for 5 games”.

3-9.title: Scale a Recipe
3-9.lead: Multiply both quantities by the same number to make an equivalent ratio.
guide: Each block is one cup. Equivalent ratios scale both rows by the same factor.
Multiply both amounts by the same number and watch the simplified ratio stay 3:2.
investigate: Chef Montoya's soup uses 3 cups of tomatoes to 2 cups of broth. Predict the amounts for 4 batches.
Set 12 cups of tomatoes. How many cups of broth keep the ratio 3:2?
Add 2 cups to both amounts. Is the new ratio still equivalent? Check the simplified ratio.
Find two more ratios equivalent to 3:2.

5-1.title: Parallelogram Area
5-1.lead: Area = base × height, using the perpendicular height, not the slanted side.
guide: The dashed segment is the perpendicular height. The slant changes the shape, not the area.
Change the horizontal shift and watch the area stay the same.
investigate: The lesson's parallelogram has base 14 and height 9. Predict its area before you build it (the model's base goes to 12).
Change only the horizontal shift. Does the area change? Why not?
Which length does the formula use: the slanted side or the dashed height?
Find two different parallelograms with an area of 48 square units.

5-6.title: Nets and Surface Area
5-6.lead: Unfold the box into a net: surface area is the sum of all six faces.
guide: The net shows every face. The faces come in three matching pairs.
Change one edge and predict which pairs of faces change.
investigate: The box is 8 by 5 by 3. How many faces does its net have, and which faces match?
Find the area of the top and bottom pair, the front and back pair, and the left and right pair.
Change only the height. Which pairs of faces change area?
Switch to the square-pyramid net. How many faces does it have?

5-10.title: Volume of a Box
5-10.lead: Volume = length × width × height = base area × height, in cubic units.
guide: One layer of cubes is the base area; the height counts the layers.
Change the height and predict the new volume before reading it.
investigate: Predict the volume of a 4 by 3 by 2 box before reading it.
How many cubes are in one layer? How many layers are there?
Double the height. What happens to the volume?
The capsule in the lesson is 2 by 1.5 by 1 ft. Use base area × height to find its volume; the model uses whole units, but the steps are the same.

2-11.title: Line Up the Decimal Points
2-11.lead: Line up the points, annex zeros, then add or subtract place by place.
2-11.context: The fuel tank has 128.75 liters. A shuttle adds 46.8 liters.
2-11.contextEs: El tanque tiene 128.75 litros. Una nave agrega 46.8 litros.
guide: Each column is one place value; the decimal points share a column.
A grey zero is annexed: it keeps the value and fills the column.
investigate: Before you compute: about how many liters will the tank hold? Round each number first.
Why does 46.8 become 46.80? Does annexing the zero change its value?
Change the operation to − and enter 175.55 − 19.35. Where do you need to regroup?
What answer would you get if you lined up the last digits instead of the points? Why is it wrong?

2-8.title: Mean as a Fair Share
2-8.lead: Level the stacks: the mean is the total shared equally.
2-8.context: Miguel earned $12, $18, $10 and $20 on four days: $60 in all.
2-8.contextEs: Miguel ganó $12, $18, $10 y $20 en cuatro días: $60 en total.
guide: Each bar is one value. Even it out shares the total equally: every bar becomes the mean.
The line marks the mean, the balance point of the data.
investigate: Before you press Even it out: what will each bar hold?
Change one value up by 4. How much does the mean change? Why?
Find a different set of four values with the same mean.
Miguel wants a mean of $16 after a fifth day. What must he earn that day?

2-1.title: Will the Answers Vary?
2-1.lead: A statistical question expects answers that vary, so you collect data.
guide: Read each question and imagine asking many people or looking at many cases.
If the answers would differ, it is a statistical question.
investigate: “How many points did our top player score last night?” How many answers are there?
“How many points does each player score per game?” Why would you need to collect data?
Change a non-statistical question into a statistical one by changing a few words.
Write your own statistical question about your class.

5-4.title: Composite Figures
5-4.lead: Split the figure into rectangles and add, or take the whole and subtract the missing part.
5-4.context: An L-shaped room: a 12 ft by 8 ft rectangle joined to a 6 ft by 5 ft rectangle.
5-4.contextEs: Una habitación en forma de L: un rectángulo de 12 pies por 8 pies unido a uno de 6 pies por 5 pies.
guide: The two methods find the same area two different ways.
Change the missing corner and check that both methods still agree.
investigate: Predict the area of the room before you use either method.
Split the room into two rectangles. Which lengths did you need?
Switch to “whole minus the missing corner.” Do you get the same area?
Make the missing corner bigger. Which method is quicker now, and why?

6-8.title: Properties Machine
6-8.lead: Rewrite an expression with a property: the form changes, the value does not.
6-8.context: 3 guitarists, 5 drummers and 2 keyboard players: 3 + 5 + 2 musicians.
guide: Each button is one property. The history names the property you used.
Watch the value after each move: it never changes.
investigate: Before you start: does (3 + 5) + 2 equal 3 + (5 + 2)? Predict, then move the parentheses.
Swap two numbers. Which property did you use?
Switch to × and try the same moves. Do they still work?
Add 0 (or multiply by 1). Why does the value stay the same?

6-13.title: Factor Tree
6-13.lead: Split until every branch ends in a prime, then write the primes with exponents.
guide: Choose a factor pair for each number that is not prime; primes end a branch.
Split a different way and compare the primes you get.
investigate: Before you split: is 60 prime? How do you know?
Split 60 as 6 × 10. Then split again until every branch is prime.
Start over and split 60 as 2 × 30. Do you get the same primes?
Write 60 using exponents. What does the exponent on 2 tell you?

6-15.title: Like Terms Sorter
6-15.lead: Like terms have the same variable: combine them to simplify.
6-15.context: Microphones (m) and stands (s) for three rooms.
6-15.contextEs: Micrófonos (m) y soportes (s) para tres salas.
guide: Each colour is one kind of term. Group like terms puts each kind together.
The check substitutes numbers: both forms always give the same value.
investigate: Before grouping: how many microphones and how many stands are there in all?
Press Group like terms. Why can 4m and 2m combine but 4m and 3s cannot?
Add a number term (no variable). What happens to the simplified expression?
Make an expression that simplifies to 10m + 4.
